lessons.title: Clearing and preparing land with hand tools vs. oxen vs. tractor
lessons.body:
Before you plant sorghum or millet, you must clear the land. The method you choose depends on your budget, land size, and available labour. Hand tools are cheapest but slowest. A hoe (jembe) and machete (panga) can clear 0.1 hectare in about 10 days of work. Use a slasher to cut tall grass first, then dig out roots and stumps. Burn or compost the debris. This method suits small plots under 0.5 hectare.

Oxen ploughing is faster and cheaper than a tractor for medium farms. A pair of trained oxen with a mouldboard plough can prepare 0.5 hectare in one day. You need two people: one to guide the oxen and one to lead. Oxen cost about $500 to buy or $20 per day to hire. They work best on flat, stone-free land. Keep the plough depth at 15â20 cm. After ploughing, harrow to break clods.

Tractors are fastest for large areas. A 50-horsepower tractor with a disc plough can prepare 1 hectare in 2â3 hours. Hiring costs $30â$50 per hectare. But tractors compact wet soil and cannot work on steep slopes or in rocky fields. If you use a tractor, plough when soil is moist but not waterlogged. Follow with a disc harrow to level the seedbed.

For all methods, clear the field 2â4 weeks before planting. Remove all perennial weeds like couch grass. If you use hand tools, dig deeply to break hardpan. With oxen or tractor, plough along the contour on slopes to reduce erosion. After clearing, leave the field to settle before making ridges or beds. Always wear boots and gloves to avoid cuts and snake bites. Choose the method that matches your resources, but remember: proper clearing saves weeding time later.

lessons.title: Making ridges and flat planting beds for sorghum and millet
lessons.body:
Sorghum and millet grow well on either ridges or flat beds, but the choice depends on your soil and rainfall. Ridges are best for heavy clay soils and areas with poor drainage. Flat beds suit sandy soils and dry regions where moisture conservation is key. Both methods need a fine, level seedbed.

To make ridges by hand, use a hoe to pull soil into mounds 20â30 cm high and 60â75 cm apart. For sorghum, ridges should be 75 cm apart; for millet, 60 cm. Make ridges along the contour on slopes. This slows runoff and traps water. You can also make ridges with an ox-drawn ridger. A pair of oxen can form 1 hectare of ridges in one day. Tractor-drawn ridgers do 1 hectare in 1â2 hours. Ridges should be firm, not loose, so they don't collapse in rain.

Flat beds are simpler. After ploughing, harrow to break clods. Then level the soil with a rake or a wooden board. Beds should be 1â2 meters wide and as long as you like, with 30 cm paths between them for walking and weeding. Flat beds are ideal for millet in dry areas because they allow water to spread evenly. But in heavy rain, flat beds can waterlog. If your area gets more than 600 mm of rain, use ridges.

For both methods, add organic matter before planting. Spread 2â3 tonnes of manure per hectare and mix it into the top 15 cm. If you use ridges, place manure in the furrows before pulling soil over. For flat beds, broadcast manure and rake it in. Make sure the bed is free of large stones and roots. Plant immediately after making beds to avoid moisture loss. A good seedbed gives strong germination and uniform stands.

lessons.title: Testing soil pH and organic matter using simple field kits
lessons.body:
Soil pH tells you if your soil is too acidic or too alkaline for sorghum and millet. These crops grow best at pH 5.5 to 7.5. You can test pH with a simple field kit that costs $10â$20. The kit includes a test tube, a colour chart, and a powder or liquid reagent. To test, take a handful of soil from 15 cm deep in five spots across your field. Mix them in a clean bucket. Put one spoon of soil in the test tube, add the reagent, shake, and wait for the colour to change. Compare with the chart. If pH is below 5.5, add wood ash or lime (1â2 tonnes per hectare). If above 7.5, add compost or gypsum.

Organic matter is the dark, rotted plant and animal material in soil. It holds water and nutrients. You can test it without a kit. Take a glass jar, fill it one-third with soil, add water to the top, and shake hard. Let it settle for 24 hours. The top layer is organic matter (floating or dark). If it is less than 2 cm thick, your soil is poor. Add 2â3 tonnes of manure or compost per hectare. Another simple test: squeeze moist soil in your hand. If it holds together and stains your fingers dark, organic matter is good. If it crumbles and looks pale, it is low.

For a more accurate organic matter test, use a field colorimeter kit ($30â$50). It measures the darkness of a soil solution. But the jar test is free and works well. Test your soil every year before planting. Keep records of pH and organic matter for each field. If pH is wrong, you waste fertilizer. If organic matter is low, your crops suffer in drought. Fix these before planting. Add manure, compost, or cover crops like cowpea to build organic matter. Healthy soil grows healthy sorghum and millet.

lessons.title: Applying manure and compost before planting
lessons.body:
Manure and compost are the cheapest fertilizers for sorghum and millet. They add nutrients and improve soil structure. Apply them 2â4 weeks before planting. Fresh manure can burn seedlings, so use well-rotted manure that is at least 3 months old. Compost is ready when it is dark, crumbly, and smells like earth.

For a small plot, spread 2â3 tonnes of manure per hectare. That is about 2â3 wheelbarrows per 100 square meters. Spread it evenly and mix it into the top 15 cm with a hoe. If you make ridges, put manure in the furrow before pulling soil over. For flat beds, broadcast and rake in. A good rate for sorghum is 5 tonnes per hectare if your soil is very poor. For millet, 3â4 tonnes per hectare is enough. Do not apply more than 10 tonnes per hectare; too much manure can cause lodging (falling over).

Compost can be made from crop residues, animal dung, kitchen waste, and ash. Build a pile 1.5 m wide and 1.5 m high. Turn it every 2 weeks. It will be ready in 2â3 months. Apply compost at 2â4 tonnes per hectare. You can also make liquid manure: put 1 part manure in 10 parts water, let it sit for 1 week, and water your seedbed with it. This gives a quick nutrient boost.

If you have no manure, plant a cover crop like cowpea or groundnut before sorghum. These legumes fix nitrogen. Plough them under 2 weeks before planting sorghum. This adds 40â60 kg of nitrogen per hectare. Combine manure with mineral fertilizer if you can afford it: use half the recommended NPK and half manure. Always apply manure before the rains start, so nutrients soak in. Never leave manure in a heap in the field; spread it. This protects nutrients from sun and rain.

lessons.title: Choosing the right planting date based on local rains
lessons.body:
The best planting date for sorghum and millet is when the rains are steady. If you plant too early, seeds rot or seedlings dry out. If you plant too late, you lose yield to drought or pests. In most of Africa, the first reliable rains come in late May to early June in the Sahel, and November to December in southern Africa. But you must use your own local knowledge.

Start by watching the rains. Plant after 20â30 mm of rain has fallen and the soil is wet 15 cm deep. Do not plant after a single light shower. Wait for at least two good rains within a week. For sorghum, plant 2â3 weeks after the first rains. For millet, plant 1â2 weeks after the first rains because it is more drought-tolerant. In dry areas with short rains, plant early maturing varieties as soon as the soil is moist.

You can also use the onset of the rainy season. In West Africa, the 'mango rains' or 'planting rains' come in late May. In East Africa, the long rains start in MarchâApril. In Southern Africa, the first rains come in November. But these dates vary. Talk to older farmers and extension officers. Keep a record of when you planted and how the crop did. After 2â3 years, you will know your best date.

If you have irrigation, you can plant earlier or later. But most smallholders rely on rain. So prepare your land before the rains. Have your seed and manure ready. When the rains come, plant immediately. Do not wait for the soil to dry. For sorghum, plant 4â5 cm deep. For millet, 2â3 cm deep. Space sorghum 75 cm between rows and 25 cm between plants. Millet 60 cm between rows and 20 cm between plants. Plant when the soil is moist, not wet. If you plant in dry soil, the seed will not germinate. If you plant in waterlogged soil, the seed will rot. Aim for a planting date that gives your crop 90â120 days of rain.

lessons.title: Intercropping sorghum with cowpea or groundnut for extra income
lessons.body:
Intercropping means growing two or more crops together on the same field. Sorghum with cowpea or groundnut is a classic African combination. It gives you two harvests, reduces risk, and improves soil. Cowpea and groundnut are legumes that fix nitrogen from the air. They add 20â40 kg of nitrogen per hectare to the soil. This helps the next sorghum crop.

To intercrop, plant sorghum in rows 75 cm apart. Between two sorghum rows, plant one row of cowpea or groundnut. Space cowpea 30 cm apart within the row. For groundnut, space 20 cm apart. Plant both crops at the same time or plant the legume 1â2 weeks after sorghum. This reduces competition for light and water. Use a 1:1 or 2:1 ratio (two sorghum rows to one legume row). Do not plant too dense. If you plant too many legumes, they compete with sorghum for water.

Cowpea is better for dry areas. It matures in 60â90 days, earlier than sorghum. You can harvest cowpea leaves as vegetables. Groundnut needs more rain (500â600 mm) and prefers sandy soil. It matures in 90â120 days. Both crops give extra income. A hectare of intercropped sorghum and cowpea can yield 1.5 tonnes of sorghum and 0.5 tonnes of cowpea. At market prices, that is an extra $200â$300 per hectare. Groundnut can give 0.8 tonnes per hectare, worth $400â$500.

Intercropping also reduces pests. Cowpea attracts natural enemies of sorghum pests. Groundnut shades the soil, reducing weeds. But you must manage carefully. Weed early. Use a hoe to remove weeds between rows. Do not apply herbicide that kills broadleaf plants, as it will kill cowpea and groundnut. If you use fertilizer, apply it to the sorghum rows only. After harvest, plough the legume residues into the soil. This adds organic matter. Intercropping is a smart way to get more from your land and improve soil for future crops.

quiz.q: What is the approximate time to clear 0.1 hectare with hand tools?
quiz.explanation: Hand tools like hoe and machete are slow, taking about 10 days for 0.1 hectare.

quiz.q: How many hectares can a pair of oxen with a mouldboard plough prepare in one day?
quiz.explanation: Oxen can plough about 0.5 hectare per day under normal conditions.

quiz.q: What is a major disadvantage of using a tractor for land preparation?
quiz.explanation: Tractors can compact wet soil, which harms crop growth.

quiz.q: When should you clear your field before planting?
quiz.explanation: Clearing 2â4 weeks before planting allows time for weeds to die and soil to settle.

quiz.q: On slopes, how should you plough to reduce erosion?
options: A) Up and down the slope
quiz.explanation: Ploughing along the contour slows water runoff and reduces soil erosion.

quiz.q: For sorghum, what is the recommended spacing between ridges?
quiz.explanation: Sorghum ridges should be 75 cm apart for good growth and management.

quiz.q: Which method is best for heavy clay soils with poor drainage?
quiz.explanation: Ridges improve drainage in heavy clay soils, preventing waterlogging.

quiz.q: How high should ridges be for sorghum and millet?
quiz.explanation: Ridges of 20â30 cm height are standard for these crops.

quiz.q: What is the ideal width for flat planting beds?
quiz.explanation: Flat beds 1â2 meters wide are easy to manage and allow even water spread.

quiz.q: How much manure per hectare should you add to flat beds before planting?
quiz.explanation: 2â3 tonnes per hectare is a good rate for sorghum and millet.

quiz.q: What is the best pH range for sorghum and millet?
quiz.explanation: Sorghum and millet grow best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, pH 5.5â7.5.

quiz.q: If your soil pH is below 5.5, what should you add?
quiz.explanation: Wood ash or lime raises pH to the optimal range.

quiz.q: In a simple jar test, what does the top layer after settling indicate?
quiz.explanation: The floating or dark top layer in a jar test shows organic matter content.

quiz.q: What is a sign that soil has good organic matter when squeezed?
options: A) It crumbles and looks pale
B) It holds together and stains fingers dark
quiz.explanation: Good organic matter makes soil hold together and leave a dark stain.

quiz.q: How often should you test your soil pH and organic matter?
quiz.explanation: Annual testing helps track changes and adjust amendments.

quiz.q: How long should manure be aged before applying to avoid burning seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Well-rotted manure should be at least 3 months old to be safe.

quiz.q: What is the recommended application rate of manure for sorghum on poor soil?
quiz.explanation: 5 tonnes per hectare is a good rate for very poor soil.

quiz.q: How often should you turn a compost pile?
quiz.explanation: Turning every 2 weeks speeds up decomposition and aerates the pile.

quiz.q: What is liquid manure made by mixing manure with water in what ratio?
quiz.explanation: A 1:10 ratio of manure to water is common for liquid fertilizer.

quiz.q: Which cover crop can fix nitrogen before planting sorghum?
quiz.explanation: Cowpea is a legume that fixes nitrogen, improving soil fertility.

quiz.q: When is the best time to plant sorghum in the Sahel?
options: C) Late May to early June
quiz.explanation: The first reliable rains in the Sahel come in late May to early June.

quiz.q: How much rain should have fallen before you plant sorghum or millet?
quiz.explanation: 20â30 mm of rain ensures soil is wet to 15 cm depth for planting.

quiz.q: How deep should you plant sorghum seeds?
quiz.explanation: Sorghum seeds should be planted 4â5 cm deep for good germination.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing between sorghum plants within a row?
quiz.explanation: 25 cm between plants allows good growth and air circulation.

quiz.q: Why is it important to record planting dates and crop performance?
options: B) To know your best planting date over years
quiz.explanation: Records help you identify the optimal planting window for your local conditions.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of intercropping sorghum with cowpea?
options: B) It adds nitrogen to the soil
quiz.explanation: Cowpea fixes nitrogen, improving soil fertility for subsequent crops.

quiz.q: What is the recommended row ratio for intercropping sorghum and cowpea?
quiz.explanation: A 2:1 ratio (two sorghum rows to one cowpea row) reduces competition.

quiz.q: Which legume is better for dry areas when intercropping with sorghum?
quiz.explanation: Cowpea is more drought-tolerant and matures earlier than groundnut.

quiz.q: How much extra income can a hectare of intercropped sorghum and groundnut give?
quiz.explanation: Groundnut intercrop can yield 0.8 tonnes per hectare, worth $400â$500.

quiz.q: What should you do with legume residues after harvest in an intercrop?
options: C) Plough them into the soil
quiz.explanation: Ploughing residues adds organic matter and nutrients to the soil.
